name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
title: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
answer: Protecting material non-public information covers the handling of facts about a company that are not yet public and that a reasonable investor would consider important to a trading decision. In an AI context this includes model performance results, unpublished benchmark scores, training data licensing deals, compute contracts, safety incidents and internal evaluations, alongside the conventional earnings and deal information. The topic sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because boards, executives and employees all hold fragments of this information at different times. It also touches disclosure controls, insider trading policy and the records a company keeps about who knew what and when.

sections.body: Protecting material non-public information covers the handling of facts about a company that are not yet public and that a reasonable investor would consider important to a trading decision. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practical infrastructure is a mix of access control, logging and communication tooling rather than any single product. Companies restrict sensitive documents to named groups, watermark drafts, log downloads from shared drives and route deal work into separate data rooms. Email, chat and code repositories are the usual leak paths, so retention rules, device management and monitoring of exports matter more than the storage layer itself. AI systems add a specific wrinkle because prompts, fine tuning data and model outputs can carry confidential facts into logs or third party services, which is why many firms now treat model inputs as a controlled channel.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is mostly classification and process discipline. Teams label information as public, internal, confidential or material non-public, set a quiet period around earnings and transactions, and maintain restricted lists that gate trading and sometimes access. Legal and compliance review draft announcements, coordinate with counsel on disclosure timing and run pre clearance for employees who want to trade. Training and attestations recur each year, and investigations reconstruct who saw a document and when. Increasingly, firms also review how AI tools are used on sensitive matters, including whether prompts or retrieved documents could expose deal information.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Obligations come from securities law, exchange listing rules and the company's own insider trading policy, and they sit with the board, the general counsel and the compliance function.Provenance matters here: a company needs to show where a fact came from, who approved its release and what controls surrounded it. Records of access, approvals and communications are the evidence base if a trade or disclosure is later questioned.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more pressure at the boundary between AI systems and confidential data. Regulators are asking how firms test models without leaking results, how vendors handle client data in training, and whether AI assisted research crosses into selective disclosure. Companies are likely to formalise AI specific rules inside existing insider trading and disclosure programmes rather than build separate ones. The open questions are practical: how to log model interactions at scale, how to attribute a leak when outputs are probabilistic, and how to keep pace with tools that make it easier to assemble a picture from many small non public fragments.
